results.title: Diagnostics and convergence assessment | Bayesian Statistics Class Notes
results.content: ## 7.5 Diagnostics and convergence assessment. Diagnostics and convergence assessment are crucial in Bayesian statistics. Trace plots, autocorrelation plots, and density plots provide intuitive insights, while metrics like the Gelman-Rubin statistic and effective sample size offer quantitative measures of convergence and chain efficiency. * Convergence forms the foundation of reliable Bayesian inference ensuring posterior distributions accurately represent the true underlying parameters. * Assessing convergence validates the stability and reliability of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations in Bayesian analysis. * Visual diagnostics provide intuitive and accessible methods for assessing MCMC convergence in Bayesian analysis. * Compare multiple chains to assess consistency and convergence across different starting points. * Compare densities from multiple chains to assess consistency and convergence. * Convergence assessment methods provide systematic approaches to evaluate MCMC algorithm performance in Bayesian analysis. * More complex models with numerous parameters often require longer chains for convergence. * Hierarchical priors in complex models can improve convergence by sharing information across parameters.

results.title: [2504.15150] Prevalence estimation in infectious diseases with imperfect tests: A comparison of Frequentist and Bayesian Logistic Regression methods with misclassification correction
results.content: [Submitted on 18 Apr 2025]. # Title:Prevalence estimation in infectious diseases with imperfect tests: A comparison of Frequentist and Bayesian Logistic Regression methods with misclassification correction. View a PDF of the paper titled Prevalence estimation in infectious diseases with imperfect tests: A comparison of Frequentist and Bayesian Logistic Regression methods with misclassification correction, by Jorge Mario Estrada Alvarez and 2 other authors. > Abstract:Accurate estimation of disease prevalence is essential for guiding public health strategies. Imperfect diagnostic tests can cause misclassification errors-false positives (FP) and false negatives (FN)-that may skew estimates if unaddressed. This study compared four statistical methods for estimating the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and associated factors, while correcting for misclassification. The methods were: (1) Standard Logistic Regression with external correction using known sensitivity and specificity; (2) the Liu et al. model, which jointly estimates FP and FN rates; (3) Bayesian Logistic Regression with external correction; and (4) a Bayesian model with internal correction using informative priors on diagnostic accuracy. Prevalence estimates and regression coefficients were compared across models using relative changes from crude estimates, confidence interval (CI) width, and coefficient variability. The Liu model produced higher prevalence estimates but had wider CIs and convergence issues in low-prevalence settings. The Bayesian model with internal correction gave intermediate estimates with the narrowest CIs and more stable intercepts, suggesting improved baseline prevalence estimation. Accounting for misclassification influenced both prevalence and covariate associations. Bayesian models with misclassification correction emerge as robust and flexible tools, particularly valuable in low-prevalence contexts where diagnostic uncertainty is high. **[v1]** Fri, 18 Apr 2025 07:11:00 UTC (101 KB). results.title: Use of Bayesian hierarchical model - Cross Validated
results.content: # Use of Bayesian hierarchical model. $\begingroup$ There is no opposition between hierarchical models and non-informative priors. My professor's notes present hierarchical models as an alternative to the use of non-informative priors in one stage. $\begingroup$ I suppose what your professor may be trying to say is that instead of 1) doing something with prior knowledge to somehow formulate some prior for a new analysis, he instead 2) embeds all information into a single hierarchical model that implicitly induces a prior. In contast, if the groups have very different means, then $\sigma^2$ will be large and the resulting inference for the individual $\theta\_j$ will be almost the same as you didn't have the hierarchical model at all. Once you have decided to use a hierarchical model for your data, there is still the question of how you will estimate parameters and account for their uncertainty.

results.title: MCMC chain analysis and convergence diagnostics with coda in R | theoretical ecology
results.content: # MCMC chain analysis and convergence diagnostics with coda in R. Last week, I gave a seminar about MCMC chain analysis and convergence diagnostics with coda in R, and I thought a summary would make a nice post. The run\_metropolis\_MCMC() function returns the posterior sample as a coda object of class “mcmc” (this is done in the line “return(mcmc(chain))”). Well, coda is an R package that provides a number of standard functions for plotting and analysis of the posterior samples. Coda is the standard package for this type of analysis, and most Bayesian packages in R use this class to return MCMC outputs, so you will likely come across this syntax whatever Bayesian code you are running. I would like to use your version (betterPairs) of the mcmc pairs plot but I can’t figure out how to add in the code to select a subset of parameters from a stanreg object generated using stan\_glmer in the rstanarm package.

results.title: Implementing Bayesian Hierarchical Modeling
results.content: ### Writing Stan Code Below is a basic Stan model for a hierarchical framework similar to our PyMC3 example: ```stan data { int N; // total number of observations int J; // number of groups int group[N]; // group indicator for each observation real y[N]; // observed data } parameters { real mu; // global mean real tau; // group-level variance vector[J] mu_j; // group-specific means real sigma; // individual-level variance } model { // Hyperpriors mu ~ normal(0, 100); tau ~ normal(0, 20); // a half-normal prior could be applied using target parameterization // Group-level parameters mu_j ~ normal(mu, tau); // Individual-level observations y ~ normal(mu_j[group], sigma); } To compile and run the model from Python using CmdStanPy: ```python from cmdstanpy import CmdStanModel import numpy as np data_dict = { 'N': len(data), 'J': n_groups, 'group': groups + 1, # Stan indexing starts at 1 'y': data } stan_model = CmdStanModel(stan_file='hierarchical_model.stan') fit = stan_model.sample(data=data_dict, iter_sampling=2000, iter_warmup=1000) print(fit.summary()) This approach demonstrates the versatility of Stan, which supports both direct writing in Stan language and interfacing via multiple languages.
